title: Why Does February Have Only 28 Days?
parts: Look at a calendar. Almost every month has thirty or thirty-one days. February has twenty-eight.
You may have heard why. The popular story says Emperor Augustus stole a day from February.
He was vain, the story goes, and wanted his month to be as long as Julius Caesar's.
It is a great story. But does it hold up?
So why does February have only twenty-eight days?
To find out, we go back to the old Roman calendar, before Julius Caesar changed it.
The ancient writer Censorinus, as summarized by Wikipedia, describes a year of only three hundred fifty-five days.
Four months had thirty-one days: March, May, July and October. Seven months had twenty-nine. And February had twenty-eight.
So February was already the short month before Caesar, and before Augustus.
Why? Wikipedia says the Romans reportedly saw odd numbers as lucky, following Pythagorean beliefs.
Here is our own arithmetic, not a documented reason. Twelve odd numbers always add up to an even number.
But a year of three hundred fifty-five days is odd. So at least one month had to be even.
Why February, and not another month? The sources we read do not say, so we will not guess.
Even that calendar had a problem. A year of three hundred fifty-five days is about ten days shorter than the sun's year.
So the Romans sometimes added an extra month. Censorinus places it inside February, after the twenty-third day.
When that happened, the end of February was reportedly cut off, leaving only twenty-three or twenty-four days.
Wikipedia also says that, by Roman tradition, February was the last month of the year until about four hundred fifty years before Christ. The exact dates are debated.
Here is our reading. Patching a calendar at the end of the year makes sense. But we found no source that says this is why.
Then Julius Caesar reformed the calendar. The new Julian calendar took effect on the first of January, forty-five before Christ.
To reach three hundred sixty-five days, it added two days each to January, Sextilis and December, and one day each to April, June, September and November.
February stayed at twenty-eight days. A leap day, added every fourth year, replaced the old extra month.
Now look at Sextilis, the month later renamed August. Caesar's reform gave it two extra days, so it already had thirty-one.
Sextilis was renamed Augustus in eight before Christ, in honor of the emperor.
So by this account, the month already had thirty-one days when its name changed. No day needed to be taken from February.
Wikipedia says the stolen-day tale traces back to a writer named Sacrobosco, in the thirteenth century.
It cites two works for that claim, by Lamont and Nothaft. We have not read them ourselves, so we pass it on with that caution.
Next time someone tells you Augustus stole a day from February, you can say the story seems to date from the Middle Ages, not from Roman times.
The short February is older than Augustus. It goes back to an older Roman calendar where February was already the short month. Why, the sources we read do not say.
So the tidy story of a vain emperor does not survive. What we can document is messier, and much older.
Small details around us often hide stories like that. Pick up a pen, and look at its cap.
Why does it have a tiny hole?
